utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-01-42-PT, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. First of all, good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Strugar, may I first check whether you can hear me in a language you understand, and please remain seated, if that's more comfortable to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I first have the appearances, that is, Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Philip Weiner for the Office of the Prosecutor. With me is Nicholas Kaufman, to my left; senior trial attorney Dermot Groome is here to assist for the day; Victoria McCreath; behind me is Gina Butler, for the Office of the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. I was informed that you have some problems also in standing, so for you the same is true as to what I said to Mr. Strugar, that if you have difficulties to stand, then please remain seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I suffered a back injury, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the Defence, appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. On behalf of the Defence of General Strugar, Goran Rodic, attorney at law from Podgorica, and my colleague, Mr. Vladimir Petrovic, from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. We are here to hear the parties in a Pre-Trial Conference, at the same time, I was informed that approximately one hour ago, or a little bit over one hour ago, a new motion was filed. Part of the problems that might arise today concern the health situation of Mr. Strugar. Whenever it comes to that, and if the Defence would prefer to have a private session, which means that you're still visible but not audible any more for the outside world, would you please indicate so that I can take the necessary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence is not opposed to public session, also when we discuss this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then of course we are not going into closed or private session unless there's a specific request to do so. But if there might come a moment, and the same is true for you, Mr. Strugar, if there comes a moment when you'd rather discuss medical matters in a private session, please let me know or please instruct the counsel to ask for it, and we'll then turn into private session. There are a few issues left from the last 65 ter conference, and already at that conference it was indicated that the health situation of Mr. Strugar was such that, as it stood at that time, it was difficult for him to travel or to move around. And fortunately, these problems seem to have been solved to the extent necessary to come to The Hague, but I do understand that this has not solved all of the problems. I read from the transcript of the last 65 ter conference that the Defence suggested that sittings would not be any longer than one hour and a half. But now, in the latest filed motion, it's not entirely clear to me whether this is still in support to reduce the time the Chamber would be sitting or whether this has a further-reaching goal. Could you please explain to us, Mr. Rodic, what exactly you're seeking, apart from what is clearly expressed in the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this motion, we wish to draw the Chamber's attention to the issue which we believe is the most important of all issues, that is, the condition of Pavle Strugar as regards his health. We believe that these proceedings cannot continue until this matter is solved. Therefore, we would like to begin today's conference by explaining this issue, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly will give you an opportunity to explain that, but I'd rather not have anything repeated what's already in your motion, because that's in writing now. And I also have to draw your attention to the following: I am sitting today as a Pre-Trial Judge in this case, but on from tomorrow, the case will be assigned to Trial Chamber II. That means that other Judges will hear this case, and therefore, some of the issues raised today might be decided by the other Judges as well. The case has been assigned today to that section of Trial Chamber II that consists of Judge Parker, as Presiding Judge, Judge Thelin, and Judge Van den Wyngaert. They are present in this courtroom today, so that they have first-hand knowledge of whatever is said during this Pre-Trial Conference. And in order to save you looking around who is where, the three Judges will hear the case are sitting to my left, just in front of the interpreters' booth. So, Mr. Rodic, if you would like to add anything to what's in your motion, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. At present, it is the position of the Defence of General Strugar that psychologically he is not fit to follow these proceedings. On the basis of the medical examinations of Pavle Strugar so far, he has the following diagnosis: A chronic insufficiency of the kidneys, an adenoma of the prostate, dementia, documented by magnetic resonance indicating multiple chemical changes, or rather, strokes of the brain, insufficiency of the blood vessels in the brain, as well as the early stages of Parkinson's disease. Psycho-organic dysfunction has also been found, arterial hypertension, chronic atherosclerotic cardiomyopathy, serious degenerative changes of the vertebrae in the neck, and coxarthrosis of both hips, where an operation of the right hip is indicated. As dementia implies degeneration of psychological, intellectual, and cognitive functions of the personality, this means that attention is poor and impaired, concentration is poorer, and memory of past events is not sure. Parkinson's disease, which is a neurological disease, as well as the chronic kidney problems from which the general suffers, which affect all his blood vessels, all this makes the degenerative process -- it exacerbates it. Apart from this, changes in the spine, in the neck vertebrae, and the hips, along with constant pain of changeable intensity, further worsens General Strugar's health condition and negatively affect his ability to follow, remember, understand, and concentrate the sequence of events. Bearing in mind that all this has been going on for several years now, and is constantly growing worse, as can be documented by medical findings, by specialists from Podgorica and Belgrade, as well as the Tribunal experts, in November 2001, who independently of one another all reached the same conclusion, I feel that on the basis of the medical documentation obtained from three different sources, the Chamber has grounds to issue a decision on a psychiatric evaluation of the general's fitness to follow the trial. As his Defence counsel, I consider that Pavle Strugar is unable to follow the proceedings. This is a brief explanation of our motion filed today, in which we ask for a medical examination under Rule 74 bis. I wish to add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, but I may draw your attention to the fact that approximately 20 per cent of what you tell us is new, and approximately 80 per cent of what you tell us is already in the motion. But please proceed and finish your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to mention that the Chamber is seized of General Strugar's health condition and has been since October and November 2001. Medical documentation was delivered in 2002, and in November and December of this year, before the arrival of General Strugar in the Detention Unit in The Hague. I wish only to add that the Defence and the general, on the 1st of December, agreed, under Rule 74 bis, but the only thing that has been done up to now is evaluating his fitness for transport to the Detention Unit. And on the 12th of December, on the general's arrival in the Detention Unit, a general practitioner only had an interview with the general, and this is not adequate treatment of the general's problems and not in accordance with our motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution want to respond to the submission of the Defence? Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to note for the record, Your Honour, that we have received conflicting reports as to the general's condition over the past two to three months, and it seems as we get closer to trial, there are new ailments that are arising. However, if there is an issue of competency, the matter has to be determined prior to proceeding to trial, if there is an issue of competency, either physical or mental.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a clear position. Mr. Rodic, you said that from three medical sources, they all came to the same conclusion. Let me just check where you said that. Could you please say in one or two lines what that conclusion was. And of course, the most important issue is whether the accused is fit to stand trial and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not whether he needs any hip surgery, for example, because if he needs hip surgery, it will be given to him if necessary, and at the time, and of course at such moment the trial could not continue because we have to stop for the hip surgery. But let's try not to confuse matters. The most important thing at this moment is whether Mr. Strugar is fit to stand trial. You say he's not. And you have referred to a conclusion from three different medical sources. Could you please briefly repeat what exactly this conclusion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what the Defence can assert before this Tribunal is that our information under the health condition of General Strugar comes from three sources. First of all, in November 2001, when the Trial Chamber was to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you, Mr. Rodic. You said, and I'm referring to page 5, at line -- is it page 5? Yes, line 9 and 10. You said: "Independently of one another," and you were referring to the three sources, "all reached the same conclusion." I would just like to know from you what that conclusion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conclusion establishing the diagnosis of dementia comes from the psychiatrist, Dr. Kmetic, from Rotterdam, if I'm not wrong, who was engaged by the Chamber in 2001, when holding a hearing on provisional release. Also as regards his chronic insufficiency of the kidneys and urological problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did Dr. Kmetic at that time conclude, that because of the dementia that Mr. Strugar could not stand trial, that it would bother him that much that he could not stand trial or was that his conclusion? I'm just trying to find out. I'm not saying that people over 60 or 70 years old might have some elements of dementia, but what was his conclusion as far as the ability to stand trial was concerned? Was there any conclusion in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Kmetic on that occasion was not called upon to establish fitness to stand trial. He was -- he only found dementia in his medical report. And no detailed psychiatric examination to evaluate the general's ability to stand trial was conducted at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying one of the sources is Dr. Kmetic and the other doctors who established dementia, and to what degree?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I did not understand your question, Your Honour, about the degree of dementia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether what other doctors concluded to dementia and whether they indicated any degree of that disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, after the findings by the psychiatrist, Dr. Kmetic, dementia was confirmed in the findings of appropriate specialists in Belgrade and in Podgorica. This was also confirmed by a magnetic resonance of the brain, in 2002. Since then, we have not had a new magnetic resonance examination, but dementia, as a disease, cannot improve. In other words, the patient's health cannot improve; it can only deteriorate further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the Chamber been provided with the medical reports from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar and the Tribunal received the latest reports from Belgrade, as well as those from Podgorica, and in General Strugar's file, in the Detention Unit, all the medical findings from 2001 are also included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just confer with the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, there has been some supporting material for your -- for some of the motions that have been filed over the last few weeks. There were medical reports and statements of doctors from Podgorica. I do not remember that I have seen any report from Belgrade. When have these Belgrade reports been provided to the registry? Has it been done by you? Has it been done by Mr. Strugar himself?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the 12th of December, on his arrival in The Hague, General Strugar had all his medical documentation with him. This included the documentation from the military medical academy in Belgrade and from Podgorica, with the magnetic resonance findings. When applying to the Tribunal for a change in his provisional release, when he was to go to Belgrade for additional treatment, medical documentation was provided on that occasion. And a complete set of medical documentation was provided on his first arrival in The Hague, because the general had been in hospital in Podgorica at the time and he interrupted his treatment in order to come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember exactly what the Podgorica report said about dementia? Otherwise we'll have to look it up. What did it in particular say?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Podgorica, as far as I can remember, dementia was certainly established, as well as the initial stages of Parkinson's disease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just, Mr. Rodic, trying to find exactly what the first report said. But that's mainly about hips. And...

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, are you looking at the findings of the 28th of November? Maybe you're looking at the findings of the orthopaedist from the clinical centre in Podgorica. That report talks about the hips and the spine, the problems diagnosed in that particular report. Together with that report, on Friday, on the 28th of November, neurologist's findings were also provided. Together with those findings, while the treatment was still under way, the Defence wanted to demonstrate the fact that General Strugar was indeed hospitalised and undergoing treatment. So that was the reason why we did not provide the entire documentation from that hospital treatment. After that, Dr. Greve provided his expert opinion as to his competency to be transferred to the Detention Unit, without going into details of his health condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that I do not find anything on dementia here, but could you please indicate exactly where to find it, because I want to understand your position clearly. Is it in the letter signed by eight doctors? Is that the one? Because I've got here in front of me the accused Pavle Strugar request for postponement with three annexes, and that's the - I would say - is the most extensive, although very much concentrating, I do agree, on the other problems, just urological problems. I'm asking you because I, as a Pre-Trial Judge, I have asked to be informed about the first findings of -- after Mr. Strugar's arrival in the Detention Unit, and it's reported to me that there's no indication that the cognitive functions of Mr. Strugar are affected. And you say he's suffering from dementia, which is a -- well, at least, it contradicts the finding of the doctor in the Detention Unit. And therefore, I'm trying hard to find a sound basis for your submissions that, on the basis of dementia, he would not be able to -- he would not be fit to stand trial. So therefore, I'm specifically looking for that. Is there anything in the Belgrade reports about dementia? Then we have to find them and to analyse them. The Chamber has never seen any report from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, General Strugar was examined by a general practitioner at the Detention Unit, and the examination was merely a conversation with the general, nothing more than that. As for the medical documentation regarding dementia, once again, I claim with full responsibility that there exists already, from 2001, the findings of Dr. Kmetic. They are at the Detention Unit. And also, the findings included in the entire medical documentation that the general has brought with him, the findings -- that is, his release letter from the military medical academy, signed by eight specialists. Now, the findings that you just mentioned of the 28th of November, they come from the clinical centre in Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, it certainly would highly assist the Chamber if you would just could give the quotes and say this is what they said about dementia and it's signed on that day by that doctor. That would certainly help. Because it seems that the Chamber has not all the material available. Perhaps we would have a break soon and try to find out what exactly is known about dementia. We could give it to the translators. And do you have copies of this medical documentation from Belgrade, for yourself, for your own ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has the copies, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you, then, please give the page on which dementia is mentioned in the Belgrade report, or the Belgrade reports, and give a copy to the Chamber during the next break so that at least we could know what is said about it, apart from what decision then to take and whether I should take a decision, or anyone else. I think that the matter of dementia is dealt with at this moment sufficiently, and you may provide the Chamber with a copy of that specific page on dementia so that we can look at it, and if you would please do the same; give a copy to the Prosecution as well. Then let's -- of course, we do not know what this all will result in. Let's try to continue and see whether there are any other problems apart from this one. May I again ask you: You said, I think it was on the 3rd of December, that one and a half hour would be the maximum time Mr. Strugar Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could be in a Court and sufficiently concentrate on matters. Is that still the same? If he would be fit to stand trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is merely our assessment, that is, if his competency to stand trial should be established, that would be our assessment. Whether that would indeed be the case, I wouldn't know. I'm sure that medical doctors, in particular, psychiatrists, that is, the specialists, could provide a better-reasoned opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And may I take it the assessment is based on your general impression?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Your Honour. So this is just a proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Then I'd like to turn to -- so no decision has yet been taken on it. I, as a Pre-Trial Judge, am seeking more information on the issues you have raised, Mr. Rodic. I'd like to move to another issue at this moment. I take it that the Defence has received the new, the third amended indictment. Is there anything you'd like to bring to the attention of the Chamber in respect of this new indictment which is, as I understand, the same as the previous one, apart from co-accused having been taken out? Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as regards the third amended indictment, we have no comments to make. We have received the indictment in the Serbian version as well, so we do not have any arguments to make regarding the indictment itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. Then I'd like to move to another issue, that is the issue of disclosure. At the last 65 ter meeting, it seemed that quite some progress had been made and that disclosure was almost complete. Is there anything at this moment, and perhaps I'm first addressing the Prosecution, is there anything still to be disclosed to the Defence which should have been disclosed already but has not been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We are moving ahead, Your Honour, with the expert reports, of the three experts, we're hoping to disclose the report or the conclusions from Mr. Pringle this week or next week and they're also finalising -- the other two experts are also finalising their reports. So we hope to disclose them if not by the end of the new year, sometime in early January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Weiner, we'll come at a later stage to the question of how much time the trial will take. I did understand that the Prosecution took the view that the trial would take some six to eight weeks. If we would start disclosing expert reports somewhere mid-January or later in January, and if, under Rule -- I think it's 94 bis, the Defence would have 30 days to consider whether or not to accept the report, wouldn't we be in a situation where experts could not yet be examined, because of late disclosure where trial on all the other elements had been finished already?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. We have to apologise. We are a bit late with the expert reports. However, we were initially told that a 65 ter hearing, there was an agreement that less than 30 days would be allowed, that three weeks would be sufficient. At a later 65 ter hearing, a new decision was made that there would be one month. So we're trying to rush them out. We're going to place the experts on at the end of the trial and try and get them in the early part of January. So there shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about how many expert reports, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One will be provided, as I said, this week or next week, and then the other two should be provided in either late December or early January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that some of these expert reports are written in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One, I believe, is written -- will be written in Slovenian and let me check on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got on my list a...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Zorc report will be written in -- the second expert, Mr. Zorc, his report will be written in B/C/S. The Defence have indicated that they would take them in any language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is the Prosecution willing to already disclose it in the original language?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're ready to disclose it to them before we even receive that translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That at least shows quite some confidence in your experts, doesn't it? And the report from Mr. Poye. Is that the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. That report will be in Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the report of Dr. Allcock has been submitted already?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's disclosed. Do we also expect an expert report by Mr. Zorc?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one which will be in B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one that will be in B/C/S. And when could that be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's the one we're hoping for late in the year or early January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What about late this year? Would that be -- I mean you're late, and I gladly accept your apologies, but I'd rather have disclosure as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will contact our military analysis unit and have them contact him and expedite the matter, as quick -- and have him get the report out as soon as possible. We've remained in contact with the experts on a weekly basis, and we're trying to get their reports as soon as possible. We have made strides to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggested this year. You said either this year or early next year. I suggested this year. Of course, I could cement you a deadline, but if you could agree on this year, perhaps that could prevent me from setting any further deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's a little bit difficult because the holiday season is coming, but I will contact the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber expects a well-reasoned submission if you are not able to file this report this year. Yes? And then still it has to be decided whether any further delay will be granted. Then finally we have I think the last report is from Dr. Pringle or Mr. Pringle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The report of Dr. Pringle is due either this week or next week, so there shouldn't be any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that will be...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: General Pringle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will be disclosed before Christmas, before our Christmas, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the Chamber then expects you to disclose it before the 25th of December of this year. Okay. Expert reports. Could we now perhaps as far as disclosure is concerned return to the witnesses. Because experts is a specific category. And is my understanding right that there were four expert reports scheduled?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are four scheduled. One has been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But no more. I mean, when I'm talking about four I've dealt with them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then about witnesses. We have seen that in your new pre-trial brief, we find a new list of witnesses, and as far as we could establish, you've taken off three witnesses from the previous list, but you've added four. The Chamber rather would see the other way around, but is our -- meanwhile, our statements or audiotapes or whatever, what is disclosed to the Defence in respect of these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We've disclosed summaries. There were a few witnesses that we were disclosing reports. I know we received two statements last week. And we're waiting, I believe, for one more interview of a military member, the chief of staff to the accused, Mr. Filipovic. And we cannot interview him without an authorisation from the government. Being a member of the military, they have to provide him with a waiver before we can speak to him. He had agreed to speak with us. We went out and visited him and he could not speak because of the lack of waiver. That's in the process and it should be arriving any day. With regard to the other witnesses, we have made all strides to provide statements or summaries. In the case of one witness, we videotaped, either videotaped or audiotaped the interview, and we have that instead of a statement. It's a long tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to hear from the Defence whether they agree with the Prosecution in this respect, that is only in respect of Mr. Filipovic, from whom there's no statement yet available, that they received -- that summaries or in other forms the content of what the Defence could expect is disclosed to them. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Defence, I wish to inform you on the current status of the disclosure. What the Prosecution said about expert witnesses, that is correct. We have received only one expert report, both in Serbian and in English, as one of the working languages of the Tribunal. As regards other expert reports, the Defence at this point has only the names of the experts. And you certainly will recall that we discussed the issue on our 65 ter conference in December last year. So, so far, in the meantime, only one expert report has been disclosed, the report by Dr. Allcock. Together with this report we have also received today your decision regarding Rule 94 bis. As regards witnesses, let me point out two issues. As regards fact witnesses, that is crime base witnesses, and the acts with which our client has been charged, we can say -- we can state that the disclosure has been completed. However, when we talk about background witnesses, the witnesses that are also very important for our defence, the other witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel be asked to slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the interpreters have some difficulties in following you. Would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I will do my best, Your Honour. In order to mention the name of this other witness, since the pre-trial brief is partially confidential, I should ask for a private session for a second, at least, so that I can mention the name of the witness so that we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into private session for a moment. Could you please wait until it's confirmed that we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it's confirmed on my screen, Madam Registrar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Then disclosure of exhibits. Is there any remaining issue in that respect? I did understand that there was still an issue outstanding or perhaps already solved, about documents stemming from the EUMM. Is that correct? Mr. Weiner, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The EUMM, previously known as the ECMM, documents have been disclosed. We have contacted them. They've indicated what could in fact be disclosed and they gave us authorisation to do so, and we have disclosed them to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that issue has been solved. Is there any submission from the Defence in respect of the disclosure of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to avail myself of this opportunity, with your permission, of course, to try and establish at this point something that I believe is very important for the proceedings. So I'm talking from experience at this Tribunal. When we have new exhibits introduced during the trial, I think that there should be a rule, that there should be a procedure on how to deal with that. We have a new exhibit, an exhibit that has not been previously introduced, there has to be a rule as to the time limit, how soon -- that is, how soon it has to be disclosed before being introduced in evidence. If I may, I should like to suggest, barring any objection from the opposing side, that two or three weeks prior to the actual use of the exhibit in the trial, this exhibit be disclosed to the opposing party so that it can become familiar with the exhibit and use it appropriately for the purposes of examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you're talking about documents never disclosed before?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. So if we have an exhibit that is completely new, that is appearing for the first time, we have had two motions recently concerning two additional exhibits of the Prosecution, which I believe will be used, and I think that this situation is likely to appear in the upcoming weeks of the trial. I think that there should be a deadline for the disclosure of these exhibits, that is, the certain amount of time should elapse between the disclosure and the actual use of the exhibit in trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we have to add any exhibits to our list, we would give Defence and the Court notice that an exhibit has just been found, a piece of evidence or a document that was not available previously. With regard to two weeks, I think that's really a case-by-case situation. If, for example, what if a photograph is found, something that you could just turn over to the Defence very quickly, show it to them, or something that they find and they want to show to us and then use? I don't feel that two weeks is necessary for proper notice. If it's a key document signed by the defendant, maybe, maybe some additional time would be necessary. But if we are able to find some documents through the JNA, the Yugoslavian national army and it takes time to obtain the document, I don't think either side should be severely punished or should be prevented from using the document at trial because a foreign government is failing to produce the exhibit or the document. I think it's really a matter for a case-by-case determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it depends what is the reason for the late disclosure and what is the content of the document involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. And whether or not there's any prejudice involved to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you rather have it on a case by case basis, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whereas the Defence would like to have a fixed term of two or three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was offered as minimum notice, because even if the exhibit in question is a photograph, it is possible that we are in the situation that we have to assess the veracity, the authenticity, of the photograph. If such an exhibit is intended for the use at trial, there's nothing we can do on a one or two-day notice. This would be our request, because otherwise we don't know how we will be able to deal with such exhibits, such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I suggest to the parties that undisclosed documents that are really of importance should not be disclosed any later than ten days before they are introduced in the examination of a witness, and that if the Defence, for whatever reason, would think that these ten days, because of the nature of that document, would not be sufficient to prepare themselves, that they will show good cause and ask for additional time to prepare. Similarly, if the Prosecution would like to use any document which has not been disclosed more than ten days before the appearance of the witness, that they should seek permission of the Chamber to use that document, and of course there again, upon good cause shown why disclosure was so late, the Chamber will decide whether or not to grant that. I emphasise that whatever provisional decisions I give at this moment may be changed by the Chamber that hears your case, but I think I could not leave you without guidance at this moment. Is there any other issue in respect of the disclosure of exhibits? Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I should have mentioned this, but I will do it now. The issue of the list of witnesses who are to testify before the Chamber, how much advance notice will we have? Just before entering this courtroom, we received a list of witnesses for tomorrow and the day after. I would ask the Chamber to take up a position on this also and to determine a minimum time period, such as seven days, for notice to be given to the Defence as to the names of witnesses who are to testify. I think this is the practice before other Chambers as well in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In other Chambers sometimes seven days prior notice, that means seven days in advance, the other party will be informed about which witness will appear and what documents, already disclosed, will be presented to that witness. Mr. Weiner, would that be a basis to work on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the parties agree on a seven-days notice. I would suggest to the parties that apart from giving the name of the witness, that they always clearly should identify whether there are any protective measures in effect in respect of that witness, that documents to be used are disclosed to the other party, and also, if this would -- if this might cause any problem, in which languages the documents are disclosed. Then I'd like to turn to my next issue. The last witness list we received, Mr. Weiner, that's, I think, a list dated the 3rd of December, 2003, introducing four new witnesses and taking out three of them. Is that the last and final list?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We filed a -- I believe another witness list on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say as part of the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As part of the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As part of the pre-trial brief. That would then be a witness list -- let me just try to find it. Do I see 44 witnesses on that list?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it also a correct understanding that viva voce witnesses on that list would altogether take 71 hours for examination-in-chief? Perhaps you would check that over the next break, because we'll have to have a break anyhow. Because after the break, I'd like to go a bit more in detail on the matter on how long the trial would take, based on that witness list. I also understood that during the last 65 ter meeting, that the Prosecution has suggested that there might be a possibility to reduce even the size of this list. What I notice is that four were added, three were taken out, which is not -- at least not what I understand to be a reduction. So could you please inform us about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We've provided the latest witness list, and we have included names on that list of persons who will not testify. For example, we have on the list both Petar Kriste and Davorin Rudolf. Our plan is to use Davorin Rudolf as a witness. Because of Ambassador Rudolf's schedule if he is not able to appear, we have left Petar Kriste on the list. We hope not to call Petar Kriste. In that situation, we will either call one or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That saves one witness, which brings it back in balance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In addition to -- there's more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We've also listed a Mr. Janicot, or former ambassador Janicot, and a Rok Vogric, last name Vogric, V-o-g-r-i-c. That is the same situation. Mr. Vogric was the initial witness. Due to certain difficulties in getting him here, we have gone to our back-up witness, Mr. Janicot, who lives closer in the area, who I believe is right now living in Geneva. So we will call one or the other. So that would reduce the list by two. We also have on the list, as a precaution, we listed a military analyst, which it has just been left kind of as an individual in reserve. That has remained on the list, and in all likelihood, as long as the military experts can testify, that person would be removed from the list. So that would be a reduction in at least three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I saw on your list, Mr. Weiner, that all viva voce witnesses have been -- at least if I look at the summaries, that you indicated how much time they would take to be examined, to be examined in chief. You also indicated that you would present an expert report of Mr. Zorc, but unfortunately, although he's listed as a viva voce witness, I do not see any indication as far as time is concerned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In the proofing chart, which is being supplied today at the request of the Court, he's listed as appearing in one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 15. It's the last name. It's to be filed today. I'm sorry. I don't believe it's been filed, Your Honour. We have them. We can file them just before the break. We can file them right now, if you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that it has been filed, partly confidential. Could that be true?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last Friday, or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. Those were the summaries that were filed. The Court had requested a proofing chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that's the new proofing chart, where we find the relation between counts and witnesses and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because on the filing of the 12th of December, I still find Zorc on page 22, viva voce witness. No estimated time indicated at all. But I do understand that today, and how much time would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One session. I take one session for four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Any other witnesses to be taken off the witness list, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, but based on -- Your Honour, based on the situation where we have not received any news on our 92 bis motion, what we would like to do is use some of the 92 bis witnesses as viva voce witnesses, including the first week in January, call one or two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We had originally filed a motion for 92 bis for approximately 15 or 16 witnesses, maybe 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Since there hasn't been any ruling for some months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can explain the parties why there has been no ruling. It was known already for a longer period of time that Trial Chamber I would not hear the case, and that it was to be preferred to have a decision taken by the Trial Chamber that will actually hear the case. And of course the new Judges have been appointed only recently, very recently. But still, we try, or at least they will try, to reach a decision even this week. I cannot give any promise because it's not me who has to do it, and I'm not fully aware of all the complications. But a decision on 92 bis will be taken as soon as possible, and if at all possible, even before the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't trying to criticise the Court on the matter. But what happens is, even if we did receive news on the last day of the session, by the time the Prosecution and investigators went to Croatia, obtained 92 bis statements or just took their current statements and had them sworn before a registry clerk, it would probably be one or two weeks into January, probably into the second or third week of trial. So what we thought we would like to do is take a few of the 92 bis witnesses that we were attempting to bring early in the trial, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. instead of bringing them as a 92 bis witness, put them on as a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. I take it that the Defence will get an opportunity to respond to that, perhaps briefly tomorrow, if the trial would start tomorrow. Then, having gone through the list of witnesses, I would suggest to the Prosecution that they will revisit the question whether or not additional witnesses could be struck from the list so that we really get to the core of the case. The case has been reduced considerably in size. And so repetitious evidence is not needed. Evidence of limited or very limited relevance is usually also not of great assistance to the Chamber. So would you please reconsider, at all times, whether the evidence you intend to present is really necessary to prove your case. The proofing charts have been filed. The new Chamber will have a look at it and see whether it meets the need of the Chamber and whether it gives the assistance as they would like to receive it. We have dealt with the witnesses. The Defence has also received, I take it, a decision on whether or not the Prosecution is allowed to call Dr. Allcock as a witness. As you may have noticed, I don't think that it's already an admission into evidence. It's finally up for the Trial Chamber which hears the case to finally decide. But on the basis of the motion, there was no reason to prevent the Prosecution from calling Dr. Allcock as a witness, and for not receiving at this moment the expert report submitted. Then I would like to have a short break at this moment, for 15 minutes, in which I expect the Defence to produce the relevant pages on dementia from the Belgrade medical report, and if there's any news as far as witnesses are concerned, then I'd like to hear from Mr. Weiner after the break. After the break, still on my agenda - but of course, you could add whatever you like to add, if it needs to be discussed at this moment - is whether there's any further cutting down of witnesses, the estimated length of trial, if we would start tomorrow. I'd also like to briefly discuss videolink witnesses, if there are any. I'd like to briefly discuss opening statement. And as far as I'm understanding, the accused would not intend to -- and the Defence would not intend to give an opening statement right after the Prosecution has done so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, that is correct. That's what we stated at the 65 ter conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just seeking confirmation of that. Did I also understand that the accused wants to give a -- to provide a statement under Rule 84 bis has not been decided yet, or has it been decided? That's an unsworn statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't recall discussing this, but I can inform you that the accused will not be making this kind of statement, either in the near future or in the following weeks and months. And the reason for this is the issue we raised at the opening of this session, and that is his health condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. We'll have a break. We'll adjourn until a quarter to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I received some copies during the break which seem to be medical reports. I would invite the Defence to guide us through these reports, to the extent possible, without having a written translation. Have copies been presented to the interpreters' booth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They have not. Could someone take care that, first of all, copies will be given to the interpreters' booth. Yes. I do understand that the booth, who is primarily responsible for the language in which these reports are written, has received a copy. Is that correct? I can't hear you because I am on the wrong channel. I think I have to go to the zero channel to get that confirmed, that the B/C/S booth has received a copy. Could I get confirmation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The B/C/S booth got the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm now on channel 6. The B/C/S booth has received a copy? Thank you very much. Mr. Petrovic, may I first take you back, before we go to this material: You said that in the documents signed by the eight doctors, that is not the specific urological or the orthopaedic report, but that we find something about dementia. Could you please indicate where it is, because I was not able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, my colleague, Mr. Rodic, will try to explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, let me first take you back, because you said it was not in the specific reports provided by the Podgorica hospital, but it was in the other general report signed by the eight doctors, as far as I understand, that we find the information about dementia. Could you please tell us where exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you can see that the report consists of three pages. In the heading, on the left, is the coat of arms of the military medical academy. So this is their report of the 9th of December, 2003. You can see this in the heading on page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I'm first taking you back to the Podgorica report, which is of late November, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there is a misunderstanding. The report from the Podgorica hospital, signed by eight doctors, was a report that you were able to see when the Defence submitted it on the 3rd of December, if I'm correct. However, this is a meeting only of the doctors' team, when the issue was the arrival of General Strugar in The Hague, and that is a ten-line document, with a conclusion that the patient's treatment should not be interrupted in order to avoid a deterioration of his state of health. When General Strugar was transferred to Belgrade, to the military medical academy, on the 5th of December, acting on orders from the investigating judge in Belgrade, specialists of the military medical academy, as far as they were able to do, because the time was very short, they gave an opinion in which the conclusion was that the general could be transferred to The Hague, with medical attendance, but they also gave an opinion on the medical documentation accompanying Mr. Strugar from Podgorica, and a small part that they were able to do at the military academy in the short time available. In the second paragraph from the bottom - and this is only the part Your Honour is interested in - the last sentence says: At the magnetic resonance of the head, from 2002, multiple changes can be seen, because of a disease of small blood vessels, which can explain the amnestic disorder present in the patient. In the next paragraph, the second sentence says: Psycho-organic dysfunctions were registered, most probably of a vascular genesis, which were not objectified due to shortage of time. Also, there is another passage which states the problem of a shortage of time. The next document, on page 1 of this document, it says: Institute for Neurology, clinical centre of Serbia. And it is signed by Vera Ilic, a psychologist, and Dr. Dragan Pavlovic, neuropsychologist. It's signed in Belgrade, on the 2nd of October, 2002. On the first page of this neuropsychological report, there are four diagnoses, and dementia is the third of these, followed by pseudoneurasthenia, which is the first diagnosis. The case history follows, then the tests used, the analysis and conclusion. On page 3, I can read you the conclusion, if you will allow me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you: You were just referring to the first page. This is the report of April 2002; is that correct? One signed by Dr. Fikret Nikolic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. That's another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm confusing two documents. Could you please repeat what document you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour, for not having a translation at the moment. The document I'm referring to is the neuropsychological report that has three pages. And on the last page, you can see the date, the 2nd of October, 2002. In the upper right-hand corner, the number 6, 7, and 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have got that one. Yes. Could you then please repeat what you refer to in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said about this report that on page 1, on page 1, the diagnosis with which the patient was referred has actually four diagnoses, the third one being dementia, and the last one also referring to a psychological problem. What follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- could we please ask the interpreters to read exactly what is written on the place where you say the diagnosis is dementia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the diagnosis is in Latin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Dementia senilis incipiens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What means that last word, Mr. Rodic? Because you only referred to dementia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means that it is the beginning of dementia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Until now, I haven't heard anything about where all the reports are talking about the beginning of dementia. I only heard you pronounce the words dementia, and always leaving out "beginning." Because you said it was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the part we have just read out, where I read out the Latin diagnosis, in the left-hand corner, it says that this is the diagnosis in the referral of the patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 we have the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then please lead me to the conclusion, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I read these six lines, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd rather have them -- if you read them, and if the B/C/S booth could follow it on paper. That's the page with the number 8 on top of it, and the date of signature to be the 2nd of October, 2002; is that correct? Yes. So if you slowly read it, and if it would be translated by the B/C/S booth. Yes. Into English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quantitative and qualitative analysis of the results obtained by neuropsychological examination shows a narrowing of the scope of visual attention, dyscalculia, dysfunction of the complex visual organisation, and constructional praxis, both in two and in three dimensions. Phonemic fluency for low frequency phonemes and a tendency of the deterioration of verbal delayed memory. This finding corresponds to a subcortical cognitive deterioration with predominant dysfunction of the right hemisphere of the large brain, which corresponds to initial subcortical dementia within the framework of (most probably) vascular extrapyramidal disorder."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand from that report, apart from details provided, that it is initial dementia? And is that the same as we find on the report of the 9th of December, 2003, where the -- on page 2 we find a diagnosis saying -- no. I'm not -- no. It doesn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the previous findings that we read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or maybe Dr. Nikolic, whom you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Nikolic also used the term "dementia senilis incipiens," which is also, as far as I understand, a beginning of senile dementia. And I checked the report of Dr. Kmetic, and that was approximately the same, that he said there could be a beginning, at least there was a suspicion of a beginning dementia. So do I understand that you're asking a psychiatric report not on the basis of findings of doctors that dementia has been established, but that a beginning of dementia has been established? Is that a correct understanding of your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the psychiatrist report of Dr. Kmetic and the fact that it has been corroborated by an MR report, MR results, the Defence would like to request, because no detailed psychiatric report has been provided so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say that the report of Dr. Kmetic has been confirmed. What actually did Dr. Kmetic say? What was his conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His conclusion was that General Strugar suffered from the initial stages of dementia. As far as I could understand, Dr. Kmetic, in November 2001, only conducted an interview with the general, on the basis of which this report was compiled. So there have been no detailed psychiatric examinations so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, let's try to get things clear. You say on the basis of the findings of Dr. Kmetic, as confirmed by other doctors, you'd like to submit something to the Chamber. When I ask you to tell me exactly what Dr. Kmetic at that time said, I'm not asking for an expose on the shortcomings of his diagnosis or the shortcomings of the examinations he made. I'm just asking you: What did he say? I'll read it to you. In the conclusion, it says, and of course we find something prior to that in the report itself: "On the ground of information raised, a suspicion that the client suffers from dementia." So there clearly he says there's a suspicion for that. And he also said: "At the moment, symptoms of dementia are at the early stage and a cognitive deficit is not very pronounced." As a matter of fact, I see that in all the reports, that there are some cognitive disturbances, although, as far as I understand, not such that a general practitioner who saw Mr. Strugar immediately noticed that there was. And as a matter of fact, in the letters that I received from Mr. Strugar, I didn't find anything specific which would have drawn my attention to any dementia, as a matter of fact. But all the reports are talking about a beginning dementia, whereas you submitted to the Chamber that on the basis of dementia, further examination was needed. I'll give it some thought at a later stage. Is there anything else you'd like to submit to the Chamber in respect of the newly provided medical documentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documentation that has been provided, that we are in possession of -- and you have now reminded me of the report by Dr. Kmetic. I must admit that I only had in mind his conclusion from 2001. I have only now remembered the details, after hearing it from you. The findings that we have just supplied confirmed the suspicion raised by Dr. Kmetic during this interview. This suspicion is further corroborated and diagnosed in this report. As to the degree of dementia, how advanced the illness is, I'm not a specialist; I cannot talk about it. From -- all I know is on the basis of the communication that we have with the general, and we do experience problems in this regard, especially in the view of what we know about dementia. Dr. Nikolic also diagnosed initial stages of the Parkinson disease. This, coupled with all other disturbances and illness of General Strugar, further exacerbates his medical condition, his physical condition. At this point, the Defence merely wishes for his competency to stand trial, to be verified, so that we can be clear whether he can stand trial or not. This is the basis on which we can proceed with the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Any observations from the Defence -- from the Prosecution, I'm sorry. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would just note that these are all more recent filed documents, that no actions have been taken up to this point, no documents had been filed over the years, and then just suddenly, within the past few months, these documents are being filed. And up to this point, they have not met any threshold to raise the issue. The issue should have been raised a long time ago, if it did exist at all. But the other question I had: Since he has been here, have they performed any sort of tests at the prison facility? I know when a defendant usually arrives, there is a battery of tests that are performed, and is there any help that we have and any information we have through the Registry from the doctors at the prison? Is my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understood, no specific additional tests have been done. But of course, it could be considered to do such tests, if they are not done. But perhaps, Mr. Strugar yourself: Have you -- Mr. Strugar, could you tell us whether you, apart from having -- please remain seated. I know that it's not easy for you to stand up, so I have no problem if you remain seated. Apart from having seen a general practitioner in the Detention Unit who examined you, have you seen any other specialist, either over the weekend or today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you tell us how long this examination has taken, approximately, when you were examined by the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this occasion, the doctor was rather forthcoming, as was his personnel, as opposed to what happened in 2001, and the examination lasted about half an hour. I don't know if I'm making myself clear. The examination lasted approximately 30 minutes. As for the first occasion, it was following an intervention by my counsel that I was given assistance. But it was only a week later, and then two weeks later, a specialist examined me. This occasion, however, they were correct in their approach. The doctor gave me -- prescribed me some medicine and listened to what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the doctor now prescribed any medicine you did not yet receive before, Mr. Strugar? Has he changed anything in your medication or ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, currently I'm taking three types of medication, three types of drugs. One of them has been prescribed for the prostate; then a painkiller; and the third one is -- I don't know what is it for. I'm taking this medicine on a regular basis, either in the morning or in the evening. But to be perfectly frank, I'm really unable to tell you what the reasons, what the indications for those medicines are. I know that one is for the prostate, but I am not sure about the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has your medication changed since your arrival or are you taking the same pills as you did before?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's only on the basis of their shape that I can conclude that this is a different kind of a medicine. Normally, they replace the medicine that I bring with their medicine. I don't think there's anything wrong with that. It must be some sort of principle that they apply. I'm not sure if I'm making myself clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be that they're not available perhaps in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Netherlands under the same form and under the same name? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all likelihood, but I'm really not sure I have given you the right, the correct answer. You should ask the doctor. I'm really not sure whether this is the same medicine that I used to take. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not expecting you to confirm that these are really the same chemical substances as you received before, because I do understand that you could not do that. I do not expect you to analyse them. You made a small comparison to the treatment you had two years ago. Do you see any major difference in how you are treated by -- or how you were treated by the doctor this weekend? Was it upon your arrival on Friday or on Saturday or on Sunday that a doctor saw you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was immediately after I entered the building. The first person I met was the doctor, and it was only after that that I met with the Detention Unit commander, or chief, whatever you call him. And this was not the same doctor as the one who actually really offended me on the first occasion. Because I had interrupted my treatment at that point. I had had severe haemorrhage in hospital, and I had arrived with a needle stuck into my vein. Because on the plane, I was being given infusion, if that's how you call it, and I kept asking for this to be removed. But this thing stayed in my vein for another week. And he even laughed at me, and I complained to my lawyer about this treatment. However, this time, it was a different person who was very polite and treated me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your information, Mr. Strugar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, maybe it would be a good idea to ask the general, since he has already explained to you what happened at the examination. You can perhaps ask him to tell you the details of the examination, and if he can perhaps tell you how he feels at this point, what his current situation is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to leave that. At this moment we are talking mainly about procedural issues, and health is dealt with at this moment mainly in the context of the procedural issues. But I'll certainly ask him about it in a later stage, Mr. Rodic. This is additional information given in respect of the motion you filed and on which a decision will have to be taken. I would now first like to return to where we were, that is, the first issue is the length of the trial. Could you, Mr. Weiner, try to set out, just in brief, how much time, all together, you think the trial would take on the basis of your present witness list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I still feel that will it will take approximately two months, with both examination-in-chief and cross-examination. And I'm talking about just the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We've maintained that period of approximately eight weeks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- all along and we continue to maintain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that include cross-examination of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And of course it's of vital importance for such an assessment of such an estimate on how much time, in your view, cross-examination usually takes, compared to the time taken by examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What we've done is just try and estimate on each witness. For example, with regard to General Jokic -- I'm sorry, Admiral Jokic, we have estimated that he would be on the stand for three days on examination-in-chief, three sessions. And he would be cross-examined, we're estimating, for two to two and a half, as many as three sessions too. With each witness we've kind of run cross-examination pretty close to the amount of time on direct examination, or examination-in-chief, as it's called in Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If we do that, the time you have given for your witnesses until now - and I'm looking at the list of 44 witnesses - is for those who will testify viva voce, it would be 71 hours, but you now also indicated that Mr. Zorc would take another four hours, that would make 75 hours. Then the time indicated for witnesses, either 92 bis or viva voce, where you usually have not given any indication as to how much time that would take --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: None of the witnesses under 92 bis would be extensive witnesses. Even if they were required to give full -- testify in full in examination-in-chief, which we don't expect will happen, the most that they would testify would be is approximately one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On your list, I find also estimates of two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Possibly two, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With a few, possibly two, but pretty much one hour apiece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I have noted down approximately what time you estimated. It comes to approximately 86 hours. And that's for the witnesses for which we have a time estimate, whereas for other witnesses we might not have any time estimate. 86 hours in chief. Let's just assume that it would need some 65 hours in cross-examination. Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately. That would then bring us to approximately 150 hours. For those witnesses of which a time estimate has been given until now. Let's just assume that those for which you have not given an estimate yet are not the most time-consuming witnesses. That would lead us, then perhaps all together, to 180, close to 200 hours. Two hundred hours, at twenty hours a week, that's five days, four hours each day, would be ten weeks. That's a little bit more than eight weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's all estimates, Your Honour, and we've done our estimates with calendars and we've come out to about eight weeks. We've done it several times, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just assume, although, of course, a final decision has to be taken on that, that we would start in December, and let's just assume that we would continue on the 12th of January, Monday, the 12th of January. That would then bring you to approximately the 5th of March. Is that a -- then I've given you a few days extra, if we would sit full time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With your estimates. Our estimates have us until the end of February. But maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So may I take it that, in view of available court time, if we would sit every day, if we would sit normal hours, that's four hours a day, effective time, that you could close the Prosecution case by -- well, let's say by not later than the 5th of March, Friday, the 5th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Based on the estimates at this time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just assume that, for whatever reasons, we could only sit three days a week. That would need then an additional number of -- well, an additional percentage at least of 60 per cent, because we are sitting less intensively. That would then bring us close to, on a schedule of three days a week. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. It should bring us somewhere towards I'd say end of March/early April, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that if you estimate eight hours -- eight weeks for the case on a five-days week, then on a three-days week you have to add 60 per cent, which is more than five weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought you said 16. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 60. I think it would bring you close to mid-April. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. And once again, these are all estimates. I just wanted to mention: Last week in the Hadzihasanovic case, a witness who was supposed to be on for an hour and a half completed his testimony after three days, and things happen, objections, motions, and we're just dealing with estimates here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes it goes quicker and sometimes it takes more time. Isn't it? Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. And also with regard to the 92 bis witnesses, which we're dealing with a large number, if there's no cross-examination on some of them, if there's little or no direct - I keep on saying direct examination - examination-in-chief on some of them, those could go very quickly. We could do as many as 12 in three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So to start with, we have a rough estimate of -- based on full-time sitting, the case would -- the Prosecution could close its case by early March, certainly not later than the 5th of March. And if we would sit on three days a week, the Prosecution could conclude its case presentation by not later than Easter. I'm just trying to figure out in less abstract terms, but just until when would it take us in this pace, and that's what the Prosecutor, although saying that it's all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. estimates, you know, most of the Chambers do not like -- of course I'm not aware of the Chamber to come, whether they like estimates which turn out to be not very correct later on, but most Chambers always very much like estimates which are real estimates and not too optimistic estimates. And that's the reason why I ask you again whether I well understood your estimates. Yes. As far as the Defence is concerned, I took into consideration that cross-examination would take, on an average, not more than 60, 70 per cent of the time of examination-in-chief. Is that something the Defence would also consider to be a right assessment of the experiences in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to assure you that we will try to be as expeditious as possible. So we hope that in most of the cases we would spend less time than the Prosecutor for the examination-in-chief. However, on the basis of what we see now, in terms of potential evidence for the Prosecution, that it is possible that we will exceed the estimated time. I don't think we should -- we could talk in percentages, but what we can do is to promise that we will try to focus on essential, key issues raised in the examination-in-chief. Whether this is going to be 60 or 70 per cent of the time of examination-in-chief, I cannot tell you, because that will depend on the individual witnesses. But this is my -- the best answer that I can give you, on the basis of my experience in representing cases before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you certainly could speak about percentages, but the Defence would rather speak about what they will focus on, and I heard that submission. Okay.
