That gives a more or less a global outline of what time the case would take if we would sit either five days a week or three days a week, and of course this still has to be further decided. I'll come back to that at a later stage. I have on my list also room for cutting down the number of witnesses, Mr. Weiner, and I dealt with it and you took off two witnesses that were introduced more or less as a pair, I would say, of which you say only one of the couple. Is there any other possible cutting down number of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Not right now at this time. As you know, the lead counsel in this case, senior trial attorney Susan Somers, is away in the United States. She had made plans to be away, based on the prior scheduling of this case. And I would not want to remove any other witnesses without contacting her or consulting with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But as we progress, if the evidence flows as we believe it will, there could be -- there could definitely be possibilities to reduce the number of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may expect the Prosecution to come back to this issue at a later stage to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Then videolink witnesses. The Prosecution has indicated, Mr. Weiner, that it intends to request a videolink for some 12 to 15 witnesses. You also indicated that still witnesses might testify viva voce, and that you'll file a motion, bearing in mind a 14-days' deadline. Because, as you are aware, a videolink takes quite some time to prepare for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're planning to file the motion this week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're planning to file the motion this week. So at least then we would have another three weeks, at a minimum, to prepare for that during the recess. We have dealt with opening statements and Rule 84 bis statements before the break. Is there anything at this very moment the parties, either Defence or Prosecution, would like to raise? Mr. Rodic, perhaps Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have listened carefully to these estimates of the length of trial, but it is quite obvious that we should also take into account the state of health of General Strugar and the length of trial will partly depend on that, I imagine, as well. It is moot as to how long he will be able to sit per day, per week, so I think that everything is relative, as far as that is concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm fully aware of that, and you will understand that it's on the basis of this that I started already with two scenarios. And of course, if needed, third or fourth scenario should be developed, but that of course is not something we could do at this very moment. This brings us in more general terms to the health of you, Mr. Strugar. At an earlier moment I dealt with your health mainly in terms of how they would influence the procedure. But I'd like to hear from you how you feel at this moment, how you experience personally your health situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must tell you: It's very hard for me to say this, but I'm not well. Let me tell you: It's only now, in hospital, that I found out that I have three vertebrae in the neck that are damaged. One of them was crushed. When this happened, there was a war on, and I had neither the time nor the inclination to put myself into the hands of doctors, for them to see what my state of health was. I went back to the front line from Belgrade and I suffered all these problems for three months I was barely able to turn around, except sitting on a chair. Now I can see that this was fatal for me. My problems with my neck vertebrae are very great indeed. I apologise for using very simple words, but very often I'm nauseous, I have pain in my shoulders, in my neck arteries. I feel constantly sleepy and apathetic. I lack energy. And this is bothering me even more than my hips, my prostate, and my kidneys, and so on. So this is what is bothering me most at the moment. At the same time, I am conscious of the fact that I must survive and that I must be here, at my age, and the position I held. And yet, I have started losing my memory very quickly. I forget what I said just a moment ago. And because of this, I feel depressed; this gets on my nerves. So when you ask me about my health, my health at present is poor. It's also poor because this is the second time that I have interrupted a therapy that was started. The first time I did this because I wanted to respond as a human being and as a soldier, and come here as soon as possible, so I did not complete my treatment. Now I started my treatment before I received the summons. I was referred to the doctors on the 11th of November. I was hospitalised on the 24th. I received the summons from The Hague on the 27th. With very great respect, I ask you to take this into consideration. I have now interrupted my therapy for only one reason, and that is to remain myself. I wish to have this over with and to tell the Court what it is my duty to say, so that the Court may reach its decision. But this is emotionally hard for me. I am an old person, so I find this very hard. When you ask me how I am, I have to tell you that I am also emotionally moved because of all this. I do apologise for speaking at such length, but my overall condition is poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Strugar. There is no need to apologise for taking some time for what is an important issue, and that is, how you feel and how you personally experience your health.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a bit emotional, Your Honour, and I regret this. I'm angry at myself for being so emotional. I would like to be calm and composed, but I can't be. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I fully understand, and I also understand that for someone your age, it is not an easy thing to appear before a court, with the expectation that you have to stand trial. I fully understand that that's not easy and that it brings --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other thing the Defence would like to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Weiner, is there anything the Prosecution would like to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to advise the Court that I had spoken with the legal officers on behalf of Chambers this morning, and they asked me to address a few of these issues, and I'll do this very quickly. What we were looking for is some of the so-called ground rules for the trial, to have some idea what the Chamber was -- how the Chamber viewed different matters and situations. For example, we're interested on the new Chamber's views on objections. Some Chambers do not like or do not care for objections and do not want them. We're also, assuming they will allow objections, what about objections during opening and closing statements? I know even the Chambers that allow free objections or open objections, they do not allow them during opening and closing statements. What about the Rules on redirect or re-cross-examination? Some Chambers allow examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and redirect, and then in their discretion, re-cross-examination. We'd be interested in some sort of idea where this Chamber would be heading. Are there any special rules for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by special rules? I would say the ordinary rules for cross-examination, such as leading questions allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Leading questions allowed. I know some Chambers are uncomfortable with it. I come from a jurisdiction that that's all we use pretty much in cross-examination are leading questions. Will there be time limits on cross-examination? I know some Chambers do that. Also, down in the future, may the Prosecution interview Defence witnesses prior to their testimony? And then the last issue, which could -- that could affect the number of witnesses is the issue of authentication. As you know, the rule of authentication here in this Tribunal is actually the Rules favour admissibility and that the issue of authentication goes more to the weight as opposed to admissibility. Will that be the policy followed by this Chamber or will we have to make adjustments to our list of witnesses and have to bring in chain of custody witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In general terms, I would say that I'll pass this list of very specific, brief questions to the new Chamber, and I think that the Chamber could provide you with guidance in that respect. I only make one observation in respect of your last question, that is, about authentication of documents. This Tribunal is not a Tribunal where a jury sits, but there are professional Judges assessing the probative value of the evidence. In such a system, a more liberal approach to authentication issues may be expected. That's the only thing I would like to say at this moment. But I have written down the list, and the questions are simple and clear, and I'm quite convinced that the answers you will get, or the guidance you will get, will be as simple and as clear. I can imagine that the new Chamber, if the trial would start tomorrow, would not find time yet before the opening statement of the Prosecution to give an answer to all your questions, but I'm sure that in due course you'll get the guidance you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no other issues on the agenda, I'd like to bring the following to the attention of the parties: A motion has been filed asking for the examination of -- medical examination in more detail of Mr. Strugar. A decision on that motion will be given by the new Trial Chamber. And although the motion has not asked for a postponement of the trial as such - at least I do not find that's one of the decisions that the motion seeks to be taken - I have considered whether, on the basis of this motion, I would have to decide at this moment that the start of the trial to be postponed. On the basis of the medical examination submitted to me, and on the basis of my personal impression during this hearing, and on the basis of the earlier submissions in writing by Mr. Strugar to me, I find at this moment no reason to postpone the start of the trial which is scheduled for tomorrow. I will, however, suggest to the new Trial Chamber that since there are only a few days left to sit in this week, and that we'll have a recess then, I'll suggest to the new Trial Chamber, perhaps in order to seek confirmation of my opinion, because it's not that much a decision, since you have not asked any specific decision in this respect, but my decision, or at least my position that I'm not going to order the postponement of the trial to start tomorrow. I'll suggest to the new Trial Chamber to see whether there will be an opportunity during the recess of three weeks, whether it's possible to get additional information on the health situation of Mr. Strugar; and if that information would clearly show that I took a wrong decision by not postponing or by not taking any decision on the postponement of the start of the trial tomorrow, the new Trial Chamber, of course, could draw the consequences out of such a mistake. But at this moment, I find no reason to decide that the start of the trial will be postponed. We stay adjourned until tomorrow at -- Madam Registrar, in courtroom --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 12.00 in Courtroom II, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 12.00 in Courtroom II.
